Master, i am tired....
So, I don’t know about you, but here in Brazil, some technical high schools require students to complete a final project. The catch? When you choose this track, you’re enrolled in BOTH regular high school and a technical program.
The program I chose was biotechnology—and I’m not gonna lie, I genuinely love it. Some classes weren’t particularly useful, but others were wonderful and helped me grow as a person. We also get access to the lab and all that cool science stuff.
ANYWAY.
Yesterday, I spent NINE HOURS in the lab. From 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. And what did we accomplish? The centrifuge went haywire (no idea what happened; it started making this ridiculously loud rumbling noise even though it was still spinning, and nobody properly taught us how to use it), we couldn’t get half the things we needed done, and we ended up making some YPD culture,and THE PEPTONE SMELLED LIKE ACTUAL HELL. I SWEAR TO GOD. That smell followed me for the REST OF THE DAY. I was already upset and a shit, this smell just had me shit and stinky.
AND THEN we found out that yeast extract ISN’T THE SAME THING AS YEAST. So we prepared the medium without the yeast extract because we thought, “Hey, if we put the yeast in the autoclave, it’ll die.” And before anyone comes at me for not looking it up beforehand: WE HAVE MORE THAN FIVE ASSIGNMENTS DUE NEXT WEEK. For BOTH regular high school and technical school. TWO OF THEM ARE MASSIVE AND HAVE A MILLION LITTLE DETAILS.
I AM TIRED.
And the worst part is that I genuinely LOVE science. I think it’s fascinating, important, and fun. But holy shit, it’s exhausting. You’re constantly tired, you end up eating like crap because you barely have time for anything, and everyone expects you to deliver increasingly complicated results, like i am fucking Hedy lammar or Marie curie..........I’m not even old enough to drink alcohol yet, and there I am producing 2 generation ethanol with minimal help.
And don’t even get me STARTED on how unfair the workload distribution feels.
The cosmetics groups—which were supposedly going to be harder—don’t even have half the workload we do. Their advisor said they could buy a ready-made mask base and add their extract, without conducting all the tests, because there wouldn’t be enough time. Fine. Whatever. That’s what I tell myself so I don’t start crying in the shower.
BUT THEN WHY CAN’T WE BUY ETHANOL, USE IT IN OUR PROJECT, HUH!? Or dunno....DUMP SUGAR in this shit to the yeast eat like the group of bioethanol last year?
We don’t have an advisor or co-advisor who can help carry out the work for us. Meanwhile, other groups have professors helping with their experiments. The phenolic extract group? A professor ran their DPPH test—or is going to run it, I don’t give a fuck. A lot of them just had to make the extract! And the bioethanol team? Fuck they, let they do a fucking Hydrolysis with cloridric acid alone!
I KNOW SCIENCE IS HARD. I KNOW EXPERIMENTS FAIL. I KNOW RESEARCH TAKES TIME. I’M NOT EXPECTING EVERYTHING TO BE EASY. BUT THERE’S A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN LEARNING HOW TO DO RESEARCH AND BEING EXPECTED TO DO THE WORK OF AN ENTIRE LAB WITH A STUDENT’S SCHEDULE, A STUDENT’S RESOURCES, AND BARELY ANY GUIDANCE, i am like, almost saying fuck you to every teacher who give us work to do.
And as if the final project weren’t enough, I ALSO HAVE A RESEARCH PROGRAM PROJECT TO FINISH. I have a submission due for the science fair NEXT WEEK, and we don’t even have half of it ready.
Our coordinator is completely unhelpful, and there are serious allegations about him that we only heard about after our advisor assigned him to us. There’s also a previous project that he allegedly appropriated, and our advisor STILL put us in a position where we have to work with him. And somehow, we’re still expected to include his name on our work.
I AM SO FUCKING DONE WITH THIS SHIT.
The final project is hell. High school is hell. Technical school is a nightmare. The research program is kicking my ass.
And the worst part? I still love science!
I love learning new things. I love the lab. I love discovering how stuff works. I love the feeling of finally understanding something that seemed impossible. But I hate how much pressure they put on students. I hate how little guidance we sometimes get. I hate that we’re expected to produce professional-level results while juggling a ridiculous number of assignments and deadlines.
I’m so exhausted I can barely cry anymore.
I just want this year to be OVER, I want to go back to my mother's womb 👹👹👹
UPDATE: The coordinator said the centrifuge didn't break!! It just gave us quite a scare because it had gone out of calibration 🙌🙌🙌🙌🙌🙌

Request for advice — dual-luciferase assay setup. PLEASE HELP
Hey everyone! I am desperate for help. I've also sent out these questions to trusted members of my committee and general support peeps, but I'm trying to cover all bases. Please let me know if you have any experience with this! You're so appreciated.
My setup: a bi-cistronic firefly–IRES–Renilla reporter (the RELITE system from Vitale and D'Agostino et al. 2025) used to screen Sec61 translocation inhibitors. We transfect HEK293 cells with X-tremeGENE, dose compounds in 96-well format, and read white opaque plates on a BioTek Synergy H1. We use a homemade luciferase reagent rather than a commercial dual-reporter kit.
We have tried altering many of the parameters, including making the reagents more concentrated, increasing transfection time, completing the assay in the dark, etc. We are trying to narrow down the issue of signal, and I have some questions for you all if I could get some input.
- Background signal. What level of background do you typically see, and how do you distinguish it from low true signal? Any advice on blank wells, untransfected controls, or reagent-only readings would be helpful.
- Transfection efficiency. How do you check it, and what do you consider acceptable before trusting the ratio data?
- Instrument suitability. Based on your experience, would a Synergy H1 be adequate for this assay, or would you recommend a different reader?
I am getting signal in my nontransfected cells that are treated, I am getting signal in my nontransfected cells that don't have treatment in them. I have high background signal in my blanks.
How should I go about testing for transfection? I am so careful about ensuring there is NO DNA in my nontransfected wells, I am so confused by this result. Why is the fricking signal the same? Are they just both not transfected? Did I accidentally get a transfected HEK293 cell line? (Borrowed the cells from another lab that also does dual-luciferase assays.)
My signal also has high variability. My SDV is broad. I had so much deviation its a joke. I literally TAKE PHOTOS of my wells to ensure they are all even at every step. I'm looking at my multichannel tips as I take up liquid. My pipetter is old, so sometimes a random tip doesn't pull, and I will GO BACK WITH A P200 AND INDIVIDUALLY PIPETTE THAT WELL TO ENSURE IT IS EVEN. I fricking refill the tip boxes with tips I know seal best because I want to mitigate error. I've been in labs for almost 10 years. Do I suck? Is it my machine? Is it me?
This assay is VITAL to my dissertation and first author publication(s). PLEASE help if you can. THANK YOU!

Best compact refrigerated centrifuge for a small clinical research site? Budget ~$5–6k
Hi everyone!
I’m a relatively new Clinical Research Coordinator at a small clinical trial site in the US, and I’ve unexpectedly found myself helping our team select a refrigerated centrifuge. My background is in medicine rather than laboratory equipment, so I’d really appreciate some practical advice from people who have used these machines.
We need a centrifuge for processing blood samples across multiple clinical trials. Our currently identified requirements include:
Refrigerated centrifugation at approximately 4°C
Around 1,500–2,200 ×g (RCF)
Runs of 10–15 minutes
Occasional double-spin processing
Compatibility with approximately 2.5–10 mL blood collection tubes
Preferably a swing-bucket rotor with appropriate adapters
Reliable temperature control, maintenance documentation, and service support
Our vendor has proposed a refurbished Beckman Coulter Allegra X-14R with an SX4750 rotor and adapters for 7–10 mL tubes. The base unit is listed at around $5,250, although we’re still reviewing the final quoted configuration.
My main concern is its size and weight (approximately 128 kg). We have limited bench space, and I’m not sure we need such a large machine for a relatively small clinical research operation.
I also found the Eppendorf 5702 R, which seems much more compact and appears to meet our basic requirements, but a new unit with the appropriate accessories costs roughly $10,000.
For those working in clinical research labs or processing central-lab specimens:
Is the Allegra X-14R overkill for a small research site?
Are there smaller refrigerated swing-bucket centrifuges you’d recommend in the $5–6k range, including reliable refurbished options?
What should we prioritize when buying refurbished — refrigeration performance, rotor condition, calibration, warranty, service availability, or something else?
How important is bench stability and vibration for a machine this heavy?
Are there any specific models you’d recommend avoiding?
We’ll verify the final choice against each study’s laboratory manual, but I’d love to narrow down the options based on real-world experience.
Thanks so much for any suggestions!

How to Improve Midiprep Yield
I was getting 10-50µg from zymo midiprep following the standard protocol, and am now getting 150-400µg (1-3µg/µL). [edit: I confirmed the yield with nanodrop and QuBit]
I have a low copy number plasmid and use homebrew NEB Stable3 cells.
I also have AAV ITRs in most of my plasmids, so I can't overgrow them like you could without ITRs.
tldr; use 5-10x the recommended culture volume and shake your tubes more aggressively for longer after adding P2 lysis buffer and P3 neutralizing buffers to ensure cells are completely lysed.
Midiprep Culture Growth: NEB Stable3 @ 30°C + 225RPM
- Inoculate a 5-10mL culture (LB+carb) with transformed E. Coli, then grow for 8h, typically until OD~=2. "transformed E. Coli" can be:
- colony picked from a plate.
- direct from glycerol stock.
- direct from chemical mix'n'go, heat shock, or electroporation transformation.
- I typically use 50-75% of recommended antibiotic, don’t think it makes a difference though. Carb > Amp.
- Make a glycerol stock by mixing 1mL of culture with 1mL of sterilized 50% glycerol.
- Make a starter culture by mixing 1mL of culture with 4mL of LB + 4µL carb; store at 4°C until no longer needed. I do this in case something goes wrong, or I need more yield; I basically repeat the next step and beyond from here.
- Put 1mL of the culture into 200-400mL culture (LB+carb) in a 2L flask (i.e. 5-10x more culture, without compromising 5-20% of flask volume). I think using 400mL cultures is probably the biggest contributor to improved yields.
- You can skip steps 1-4 and it won't make any difference (I've only tested this after electroporation transformation, but that does get incubated for 1h before I put it into a 400mL culture).
- Grow until OD 2-2.5 (sometimes I come in late and it's ~3; i've found this gives higher yield but doesn't seem to recombine the ITRs based on plasmidsaurus ONT). And yes, I check the OD every time; it takes at all then you haven’t spun long enough and are pouring out good bacteria.
- Pour out supernatant. Sometimes the pellet loosens so if you see that happening you have to stop pouring and re-spin so you don’t loose bacteria. I normally pour the supernatant back into the 2L flask it came from, just in case I messed something up, I can just pour it back into the 240mL tube and re-spin. You can leave a small amount (I think this is also another major factor in yield improvement: making sure your cells are fully lysed.
- Use 25-50% more B2 and B3 buffer than suggested. Probably binding buffer too. I admit adding 50% more solution is basically like doing a maxi, and you're also consuming reagents for future preps, so I only do this if we magically have extra buffer leftover from older kits.
- Spin 10min @ 3500g after the P3 yellow buffer following the “low copy number protocol”. Use a p1000 pipette tip to hold the floating lysis crud while you pour the supernatant into the syringe
- Warm elution buffer to 55°C, and let it sit on the matrix for 5-10minutes before spinning.
- I use the recommended 200µL of elution buffer for midi.
- I use ultra pure H20 as the elution buffer so that I can electorporate mammalian cells with it, the elution buffer supplied or TE buffer has salts that may cause arcing.
- Double elute with the same elution buffer (i.d. suck it up from your 1.5mL tube and put it back on the matrix and spin again).
- I find that I end up with 160-180µL afterwards. 20-40µL being lost to the elution gods after the two elution spins.
- If you need higher concentrations, you can leave the tube open overnight (can take a couple days depending on your desired concentration) to let water evaporate or use a SpeedVac vacuum concentrator.
- If you do this, be sure to elute with UP H20, otherwise the salt concentration will increase because the salts won't evaporate with the water.
This probably applies to maxiprep too, but I'd do 1-2L of culture and expect >1mg of DNA. I haven't tried it though.
Some of these tips I got from various other reddit posts (i.e. credit to this one), but these are all compiled together and I've verified it with 10+ midipreps within the last week.
Let me know if you have feedback and I can update the list, as I'm sure my goldfish memory will google "how to improve midiprep yield" in 6 moths.

How do you reach US students for a European PhD program? Hoping for some advice
Hi r/labrats,
I hope posts like this are allowed here. If not, mods, feel free to remove it.
I coordinate ORFeus, an EU-funded PhD network (MSCA Doctoral Network) with 15 fully funded PhD positions across Europe. The research is on microproteins and the dark proteome: Ribo-seq, proteomics, immunopeptidomics, AI, etc.
Our problem is that almost no US students apply. Over 10 US professors in the field are helping us: posters on their campuses, emails to their departments, forwarding the call to colleagues and students. We’ve also posted on JobRxiv, the Genetics Society of America, LinkedIn, Indeed, PhDScanner and FindAPhD (and more). Applications are coming in from Europe, Asia and elsewhere, but from the US we get close to nothing. Any nationality can apply, and these are salaried positions with benefits, not stipends.
One thing that did not help at the start is that we mentioned that positions require an MSc or 'equivalent', which is the formal language the EU recommends, but as I have now learned rarely applies to US students. They do a BSc, do some years in lab rotations, etc., and in the end EU institutes can make exceptions for these candidates, as they clearly have that 'equivalent' experience. We changed this in follow-up advertisements, but to no avail.
So I would love to hear from anyone who’s been through this. Students, PhDs, postdocs, PIs: how would you get a call like this in front of US students? And if you’re a student, what would make you skip it?
Thanks a lot, any advice is welcome.
Edit: To clarify, since a few people asked: we are not looking for US students in particular, and nationality plays no role in selection. We simply want to reach as many potentially excellent candidates as possible, wherever they are from, and we get good applicants from many countries worldwide so we are happy to see that there seems to be a global reach. The US is the one place where almost nothing comes in, despite a lot of effort through US colleagues. I am trying to understand whether that is down to our approach, whether it is just to be expected for European PhDs, or whether there is something we could do differently.

Problem with RNase inhibitor (SUPERaseIn)
We're testing whether a detection signal is RNA-dependent. We split each sample into three and treat in parallel:
1. DNase (expect signal)
2. RNase cocktail, A (500 U/mL) + T1 (20.000 U/mL) (expect loss of signal)
3. RNase cocktail (A + T1) + SUPERase•In (20.000 U/ml) (expect rescue)
Problem: the inhibitor doesn't rescue. After cleanup (column, and also TRIzol + precipitation, tested both) e.g. starting from 200 ng/µL we measure in same volumes:
DNase: 187 ng/µL
RNase: 0.3 ng/µL
RNase + SUPERase•In: 0.2 ng/µL
Already tried:
Proteinase K treatment (10 min) after digest, in case RNase-inhibitor complexes were clogging the column
Pre-incubating RNase and inhibitor for 30 min at 25 °C before adding to the RNA
Raising inhibitor:RNase ratio to 8:1
Glycerol-only control (same amount as in the inhibitor storage buffer) to check for effects on column binding
TRIzol + precipitation instead of column cleanup
Different new aliquot of Inhibitor
Adding only Inhibitor & no RNase (no loss observed).
Nobody in our lab has worked much with RNA beyond occasional isolations, so we're a bit stuck. Is there something obvious we're missing?

PFA question for immunostaining / in situ
Hello everyone,
I’m a biology PhD student working on characterizing the interaction between two interacting proteins. To do this, I will use a proximity ligation assay, which allows us to detect the existence, prevalence, and approximate distance of this interaction in situ, which can then be visualized later. The assay uses primary antibodies and proprietary probes, which bind to the antibodies to detect your proteins of interest when they are interacting.
The tissue sections I'll use for this were mounted on cover glasses without PFA. I’ve never done immunostaining before, so I’m trying to understand what this means for my experiment. Do I need to add PFA to these slides and then dewax them? Or do I skip this redundancy because the PFA isn’t there? The proximity assay protocol doesn’t tell you whether PFA is ever necessarily required, but I’ve read that other groups have used it as a natural fixation technique for tissues (my tissue slides did not use PFA because they were originally meant to be used with RNAscope but were unused, so I’m using them). Let me know what you think!

Triton-X alternative for bacterial cell lysis and DNA extraction
tl;dr I need to stop using Trixon-X100 in for bacterial DNA extraction because it's getting hard to buy - please suggest alternatives that aren't Tween
I run an undergraduate lab practical in which we use a standard STET buffer recipe - 10mM Tris-HCl, 1mM EDTA, 100mM NaCl and 5% Triton* X- 100. We need undergraduates to extract plasmid DNA from a bacterial cell pellet.
I would like to replace the Triton-X 100 component in two places: the initial resuspension of bacteria in STET, and the follow on STET+lysozyme step. Lots of students adds up to quite a lot of STET over time.
As I understand it, swapping for TWEEN-20 is likely to reduce the DNA yield. For undergraduates who sometimes manage to get low yields, this makes TWEEN-20 unattractive. I can't use anything that will reduce the lysozyme activity either.
Because Triton-X is pretty nasty for the environment, I need to fill out paperwork every time I want to buy it, and I think it's time to just replace it in this specific use-case.

But it feels like everyone else in the lab are always busy and doing more wet lab work than I am. Not only that but I feel like everyone is just… better at managing their time than I am? It’s not like I’m new either, I’ve been in this lab for several years (though to be fair I’m still in the first couple years of my PhD).
I also was recently diagnosed with AuDHD and OCD, and combined with some external life stressors it’s caused me to mess up more than I usually do in my experiments. My PI also pointed this out to me and literally asked me what types of lab work I liked and didn’t like to help tailor my project to my strengths, since she saw my project had been stagnating a while. Which is exactly what a PI should do (and truly I feel like I lucked out even working in this lab), but I can’t help but feel like I’m this person in the lab who is “special needs”, who needs shit catered to them, who can’t parallel process and manage multiple experiments at once like other grad students can, etc. I’m supposed to be one of the senior students in the lab, but I feel like I’m the clown in a space filled with professionals.

My PI has been heavily pushing me to get a paper out of my work. Which again, is a good thing, but on the flip side I can’t help but feel like they’re giving me extra help because I can’t do shit on my own like everyone else can. Masters students have come and gone and had papers published on their work, my peers in my lab produce such nice quality work at a steady pace to where they always have something to bring to lab meetings. But I feel like I’m just… not that. I’m the one dragging the lab behind and it’s a wonder that my PI hasn’t brought me into their office and told me I should reconsider being a PhD student yet.
I know impostor syndrome is common when doing a PhD, but I don’t know… it feels more like I’ll never have the discipline and the work ethic to pace myself to get nice experiments done, and that I’ll always just exist to sap up money from my lab that could go to another student who’s actually ready for a PhD. And it sucks because for years I’ve dreamed to get here. I genuinely don’t know what I’d be doing if not a PhD. My Asian parents still insist I can go into medicine and I’ve kept turning them down all so I can continue this work. But what if I’m just not cut out for it? What if I am just ruining my life?

HepG2 cells revival
Has anyone had any issue reviving HepG2 cells from ECACC UK?
- i revived as soon as they arrived in a 37deg water bath, with the tube inside a sterile tube, until just completely thawed
- transferred immediately into 9ml warmed complete 10% FBS DMEM plus NEAA, Glutamax, pyruvate, penstrep, counted cells and centrifuged at 90g for 10min
- Replaced supernatant with 10ml complete media as above
- they were >90% viable upon counting, and at the recommended seeding density for this cell line for a T75
The cells took many days to attach, and even then I only had enough attached cells by day 6, when I changed the media this time to the equivalent of 10% FBS EMEM with the same supplements as above. Changed media every 3 days. It’s now been 2 weeks and I have very few colonies of cells, which have only just started proliferating
All my other cell lines are growing fine - multiple HEK cell lines, THP-1s
ECACC are saying the DMEM is the issue and they should have been revived in EMEM. However there are heaps of publications using DMEM to culture HepG2?
